title: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition
authors: Kaiming He, Xiangyu Zhang, Shaoqing Ren, Jian Sun

pages.title: The core idea
pages.subtitle: Make very deep networks easy to train

blocks.html: Before this paper, stacking more layers onto a convolutional network often made it worse, not just at test time but on the training set too. That was surprising: a deeper model can in principle copy a shallower one and add identity layers, so it should never do worse. ResNet's insight is that the problem is one of optimization — very deep plain networks are simply hard for gradient descent to fit.

The fix is a residual learning framework. Instead of asking a few stacked layers to learn a desired mapping $H(x)$ directly, we ask them to learn the residual $F(x) = H(x) - x$, and then add the input back: the layers output $F(x) + x$. If the best thing to do is nothing, the network just has to push the weights toward zero, which is far easier than learning an identity through nonlinear layers.
We explicitly reformulate the layers as learning residual functions with reference to the layer inputs, instead of learning unreferenced functions.

With this one change the authors trained networks of unprecedented depth. A 152-layer ResNet won the ILSVRC 2015 classification challenge, and an ensemble reached 3.57% top-5 error on ImageNet — while still being lower in computational complexity than VGG. The same idea also won detection and segmentation tracks, showing it is a general-purpose building block, not an ImageNet trick.

A natural expectation is that adding layers can only help, since extra layers could learn to do nothing. In practice the opposite was observed: as plain networks got deeper, accuracy saturated and then degraded rapidly. Crucially this is not overfitting — the training error also goes up. A 56-layer plain net had higher training error than a 20-layer one.

This tells us the issue is not capacity but trainability. Deep stacks of nonlinear layers struggle to approximate even the identity mapping, so the solver cannot find a solution that is at least as good as the shallower network it contains.

If the optimal function for some block is close to the identity, a residual block only needs to drive $F(x)$ toward zero. Zero is a comfortable place for weight matrices to sit. Learning an exact identity by composing several ReLU and convolution layers, by contrast, requires a precise nonlinear conspiracy. Residual connections give the optimizer an easy default to fall back on.

pages.title: The residual block
pages.subtitle: A shortcut that adds the input back

blocks.html: The building block takes an input $x$, runs it through a couple of weight layers to produce $F(x)$, and then adds the untouched input through a shortcut (skip) connection:

Reading this: $y$ is the block output, $F(x, \{W_i\})$ is the residual learned by the stacked layers (for two layers, $F = W_2\,\sigma(W_1 x)$ with $\sigma$ the ReLU), and the $+\,x$ term is the identity shortcut. The shortcut adds no parameters and almost no compute, so residual nets cost the same as their plain counterparts.
When $F$ and $x$ have different dimensions (for example when the number of channels changes), the shortcut applies a linear projection $W_s$ so the addition is well defined:

The element-wise sum is followed by a final ReLU. Because the gradient of the addition flows straight through the identity branch, signals can reach early layers undiminished — this is why very deep ResNets stay trainable.

pages.title: Going very deep: the bottleneck
pages.subtitle: 1x1 convolutions to stay cheap at 50+ layers

blocks.html: To reach 50, 101, and 152 layers without exploding the cost, the authors replace the two-layer block with a bottleneck design: a $1\times1$ convolution that reduces the channel dimension, a $3\times3$ convolution that does the spatial work on the smaller representation, and a $1\times1$ convolution that restores the dimension.

items: $1\times1$ conv: squeeze channels (e.g. 256 → 64) so the expensive $3\times3$ runs on a thin tensor.
$3\times3$ conv: the actual feature extraction, now cheap.
$1\times1$ conv: expand back (64 → 256) so the shortcut sum lines up.

blocks.html: Here the parameter-free identity shortcut matters even more: if the shortcut had to be a projection, it would connect the two high-dimensional ends and double the block's size. Keeping it identity is what makes deep bottleneck models efficient.

On ImageNet the plain-vs-residual comparison is decisive. A plain 34-layer net does worse than a plain 18-layer net (the degradation problem), but the residual 34-layer net beats the residual 18-layer net and trains faster. Adding depth now helps, exactly as intuition originally suggested.

Pushing to extreme depth, ResNet-152 had the lowest single-model error, and the winning ensemble reached 3.57% top-5 error on the ImageNet test set — first place in ILSVRC 2015. Notably, the 152-layer model still has lower complexity (FLOPs) than the much shallower VGG-16/19.

On CIFAR-10 the authors trained networks past 1000 layers to probe the limits of optimization; even a 110-layer ResNet trains cleanly where a plain net of that depth fails. This is direct evidence that residual learning addresses an optimization problem, not just a regularization one.

The same backbone, dropped into the detection pipeline, also won the COCO 2015 and ImageNet detection and localization tracks. Replacing a VGG backbone with ResNet-101 gave large gains in mAP essentially for free, which is why ResNet became the default feature extractor across computer vision.
Solely due to our extremely deep representations, we obtain a 28% relative improvement on the COCO object detection dataset.

ResNet did more than win a competition: it made depth a usable resource. The skip connection is now a near-universal component — it appears in DenseNets, U-Nets, and, importantly, inside the Transformer, where every attention and feed-forward sub-layer is wrapped in a residual connection for the same reason: to let gradients flow through very deep stacks.

items: Residual learning reframes the target as $F(x)=H(x)-x$, making identity-like mappings trivial to learn.
Identity shortcuts add no parameters and let gradients bypass nonlinear layers.
Enabled 152-layer (and 1000+ on CIFAR) networks with state-of-the-art accuracy at lower cost than VGG.
Became the standard backbone for detection, segmentation, and beyond.
